q: 1. The direction of shear stress is
explain: Shear stress can act in both horizontal and vertical planes depending on the loading conditions and the orientation of the cross-section being analyzed.

q: 2. The direction of normal stress is
explain: By definition, normal stress acts perpendicular (normal) to the surface of the cross-section or failure plane.

q: 3. The direction of shear stress is
explain: Unlike normal stress, shear stress acts tangential or parallel to the surface of the plane.

q: 4. The actual numerical value of tensile stress (engineering stress) is .............. than the theoretical stress
explain: Engineering stress is calculated using the original cross-sectional area, whereas theoretical (true) stress accounts for the reduction in area during tension.

q: 5. Allowable stress in steel is less than
explain: For safety, the allowable or working stress is always kept significantly lower than the yield stress of the material to prevent permanent deformation.

q: 6. According to Hook's law, which one is wrong?
explain: Hooke's Law states Stress = E × Strain. Therefore, MoE × Stress = Strain is mathematically incorrect.

q: 7. Stress is directly proportional to strain within elastic limit is given by
explain: This fundamental principle of elasticity was established by Robert Hooke.

q: 8. Elasticity of a body is defined
options: the property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of load
the property by which a body don't returns to its original shape after removal of load
the property by which a body undergoes deformation even after removal of load
explain: Elasticity is the physical property that allows a material to return to its original dimensions after the unloading process.

q: 9. Elasticity of a body is
options: the ratio of stress to strain
the resistance to the force acting
explain: Elasticity represents the internal resistance of the material molecules to being separated by an external force.

q: 10. Permanent set is
options: the force which acts permanently on the body
the shape of the member just after completion of construction
ratio of poisson's ratio to young's modulus
explain: Permanent set refers to the plastic deformation that remains in a body after the applied stress is removed.

q: 11. Stress in a member subjected to a force is
options: the ratio of modulus of elasticity to strain
the product of modulus of elasticity and strain
the resistance to the force acting
sum of strain and modulus of elasticity
explain: According to the constitutive relation σ = Eε, stress is the product of the modulus of elasticity and strain.

q: 12. Young's modulus is the ratio of the normal stress to the
options: reciprocal of normal strain within elastic limit
explain: Young's modulus is valid only within the proportional limit where the stress-strain curve is linear.

q: 13. Modulus of rigidity is the ratio of
explain: The modulus of rigidity (G) is the ratio of shear stress to the corresponding shear strain.

q: 14. In any member of structure system, the strain does not effect the size of member
explain: Shear strain involves a change in shape (angle) rather than a change in dimensions or volume.

q: 15. Plasticity of a body is
options: the ratio of stress to strain
explain: While elasticity allows recovery of shape, plasticity is the property that allows permanent deformation.

q: 16. The ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain is called
explain: Poisson's ratio is a dimensionless constant representing the ratio of transverse contraction to longitudinal extension.

q: 17. The product EI is called
explain: The product of Young's modulus (E) and Moment of Inertia (I) defines the bending resistance of a beam, known as flexural rigidity.

q: 18. The value of possion's ratio always remains
explain: For most engineering materials, Poisson's ratio typically ranges from 0 to 0.5, thus remaining less than one.

q: 19. The percentage elongation of a material from a direct tensile test indicates
explain: High percentage elongation is a primary indicator that a material is ductile and can undergo significant plastic deformation.

q: 20. The percentage reduction of a material from a direct compressive test indicates
explain: Similar to elongation in tension, reduction in cross-sectional area in compression is a measure of ductility.

q: 21. The safe value of stress below which the material will not fail when subjected to reversal of stress is known as
explain: Endurance limit is the maximum stress that a material can withstand for an infinite number of cycles without failure.

q: 22. The property by which the metals deforms continuously at a slow rate without further increase in stress is called
explain: Creep is the time-dependent permanent deformation that occurs under constant stress, usually at high temperatures.

q: 23. Toughness is
options: ability to absorb energy during plastic deformation
explain: Toughness represents the total energy a material can absorb before it actually fractures.

q: 24. The impact tests are used to determine
explain: Tests like Charpy and Izod measure the energy absorbed during impact, which defines the toughness.

q: 25. The ratio of maximum instantaneous stress due to sudden loading to the maximum stress due to gradual loading will be
explain: Stress produced by a suddenly applied load is twice the stress produced by the same load applied gradually.

q: 26. What is tenancy?
explain: Tenacity (often misspelled as tenancy) refers to the ultimate tensile strength of a material.

q: 27. At ordinary temperatures, how is the yield point affected with rate of loading?
explain: At normal room temperatures, the rate of loading has a negligible effect on the observed yield point.

q: 28. Simple bending equation is
explain: This is the standard Euler-Bernoulli bending equation relating moment, inertia, stress, and curvature.

q: 29. Stress in a beam due to simple bending is
explain: Bending stress is directly proportional to the distance from the neutral axis (y).

q: 30. In a composite bar the load distribution among different materials of which it is made is based on the assumption the all the materials will have
explain: In composite bars, the primary assumption for compatibility is that all components undergo the same amount of strain.

q: 31. The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
explain: Thermal stress only develops if the expansion or contraction is restricted by the support conditions.

q: 32. Strain energy of a member may be defined as work done on it
explain: Strain energy is the internal work stored in a material due to any form of deformation (tension, compression, etc.).

q: 33. Partial derivative of strain energy gives
explain: According to Castigliano's first theorem, the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to a load gives the deflection at that load.

q: 34. The strain energy stored in a specimen when strained within the elastic limit is known as
explain: Resilience is the capacity of a material to absorb energy when it is deformed elastically.

q: 35. The maximum strain energy stored in a specimen when strained within the elastic limit is known as
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum energy that can be stored without causing permanent deformation.

q: 36. Find the elongation of a rod if a load of p is applied on a rod having length, l c/s area, A and modulus of elasticity, E
explain: The standard formula for axial deformation is derived from Hooke's Law (σ = Eε), where strain ε = Δl/l and stress σ = p/A.

q: 37. Find the modulus elasticity of bar material (E) if c/s area of bar is A, length L, applied load P and elongation is Δ
explain: Rearranging the elongation formula Δ = PL/AE to solve for E gives E = PL/AΔ.

q: 38. The amount of stress developed due to increase in temperature in case of SSB if l=10m, ΔT=10°C, A=5cm²
explain: As per key 1 but In a Simply Supported Beam (SSB), the beam is free to expand or contract. Since there is no restriction to thermal expansion, no thermal stress is developed.

q: 39. A member having cross section 5 cm × 5 cm is subjected to a tensile stress of 100 kg/cm², then the applied load should be
explain: Load = Stress × Area. Area = 5cm × 5cm = 25cm². Load = 100 kg/cm² × 25cm² = 2500 kg.

q: 40. Torsion is produced in a beam due to
options: eccentricity of load from centroidal axis
explain: Torsion occurs when a load is applied at a distance (eccentricity) from the longitudinal centroidal axis, creating a twisting moment.

q: 41. Due to torsion moment beam get
explain: While bending moments cause curvature (bending), torsional moments specifically cause the cross-sections to rotate or twist relative to each other.

q: 42. Torsional equation is given by
explain: This is the standard torsion formula relating torque (T), polar moment of inertia (J), shear stress (τ), radius (R), modulus of rigidity (C), angle of twist (θ), and length (l).

q: 43. The amount of temperature stress is .......... in fixed beam if compared with propped cantilever.
explain: A fixed beam provides total constraint at both ends, whereas a propped cantilever may allow some relief of stress depending on the specific support conditions and degrees of freedom.

q: 44. If the M.I of section about its axis is I and if the effective sectional area is A, then radius of gyration r is given by
explain: The radius of gyration is defined as the distance from the axis at which the entire area could be concentrated to yield the same moment of inertia: I = Ar².

q: 45. Stress concentration near the void is ................ as compared to solid portion.
explain: Voids or discontinuities disrupt the flow of stress lines, causing them to 'bunch up' and increase the local stress intensity.

q: 46. Hoop stress is
explain: In thin-walled cylinders under internal pressure, hoop stress acts along the circumference and is tensile in nature.

q: 47. The moment of inertia of rectangular section is
explain: For a rectangle of breadth B and depth D, the moment of inertia about the centroidal x-axis is BD³/12.

q: 48. Ratio of moment of inertia (MOI) of a rectangular object about its x-axis to its base is
explain: MOI about centroid is BD³/12. MOI about base is BD³/3. The ratio (BD³/12) / (BD³/3) = 1/4.

q: 49. M.I of circular section
explain: The moment of inertia for a circle of diameter d about any centroidal axis is πd⁴/64.

q: 50. The moment of inertia of square section is
explain: A square is a rectangle where B = D = a, so BD³/12 becomes a⁴/12.

q: 51. The moment of inertia of elliptical section is
explain: For an ellipse with major axis B and minor axis D, the formula follows the π/64 convention similar to circular sections.

q: 52. The moment of inertia of triangular section about its c.g.
explain: While the MOI of a triangle about its base is bh³/12, the MOI about the centroidal axis parallel to the base is bh³/36.

q: 53. Along the neutral axis of a simply supported beam
explain: By definition, the neutral axis is the layer where bending stress and strain are zero.

q: 54. The ratio of the moment of inertia of a circular plate and a square plate for equal depth is
explain: Comparing (πd⁴/64) for the circle and (a⁴/12) for the square where d = a leads to the mathematical ratio 3π/16.

q: 55. The section modulus of a rectangular section is proportional to
options: square of the area of the section
product of the area and depth
product of the area and width
explain: Section Modulus Z = BD²/6. Since Area A = BD, Z can be expressed as (A × D)/6, showing proportionality to area.

q: 56. The algebraic sum of the vertical forces on either side of the section of a loaded beam is known as
explain: Shear force at any section is the net vertical force acting on one side of that section.

q: 57. Find the shear force produced in the member BC due to load shown in fig.
explain: Based on the figure, the vertical load applied at C is 4 kN, which remains constant through the member BC.

q: 58. Find the bending moment at fixed end for the structure as shown in fig.
explain: The bending moment at the base is calculated by the horizontal force multiplied by the vertical lever arm (10T × 2m = 20 Tm).

q: 59. Find the bending moment at fixed end for the structure as shown in fig.
explain: In this specific geometry, the moments from the opposing loads cancel each other out at the fixed end.

q: 60. Find the bending moment at fixed end of cantilever as shown in fig.
explain: The moment is calculated by the sum of forces times their distances (5T × 2m + 10 Tm = 20 Tm).

q: 61. Find the bending moment at fixed end of cantilever as shown in fig.
explain: Similar to Q60, but with different force/distance values: the net moment at the wall is 10 Tm.

q: 62. A rectangular beam carries a maximum bending moment of M. If its depth is doubled, its moment carrying capacity will be
explain: Moment capacity is proportional to the Section Modulus Z (BD²/6). If D is doubled (2D), Z becomes B(2D)²/6 = 4BD²/6, increasing capacity 4 times.

q: 63. The algebraic sum of the moments of the forces on either side of the section of a loaded beam is known as
explain: This is the formal definition of the internal bending moment at a specific point in a beam.

q: 64. The shear force and bending moment are related by
explain: The rate of change of the bending moment (dM/dx) at any section is equal to the shear force (V) at that section.

q: 65. The shear force on a beam and the displacement are related by
explain: Bending Moment M = EI(d²y/dx²). Since V = dM/dx, it follows that V = EI(d³y/dx³).

q: 66. Which one is correct if the deflection of a beam is y
explain: The slope (θ) of a beam's elastic curve is the first derivative of the deflection (y) with respect to x.

q: 67. Calculate the maximum BM introduced due to a udl of 4KN/m, if the span of the cantilever is 1.8m
explain: Maximum BM for a cantilever with UDL is wL²/2. (4 × 1.8²) / 2 = 6.48 KN-M.

q: 68. Find the bending moment at 1/4th of the span having simply supported beam with following data: point load = 200 kg at centre, span = 20m
explain: Reaction at support is 100 kg. At x = 5m (1/4th span), BM = 100 kg × 5m = 500 kg-m.

q: 69. The maximum deflection in the cantilever beam subjected to an udl of W /m throughout the span is
explain: This is a standard deflection formula for a cantilever beam under a uniformly distributed load.

q: 70. A simply supported beam of length l carries a load varying uniformly from zero at left end to maximum at right end maximum bending moment occurs at a distance of
explain: For a triangular load, the maximum moment occurs where shear force is zero, which is at a distance of l/√3 from the apex (zero load end).
